summary: An inductively heated atomic oven achieves a 7.65× improvement in heating rate compared to resistive heating, reaching the 773 K target temperature in 4.33 minutes versus 33.13 minutes, and demonstrates stable operation to 1273 K with temperature fluctuations below ±2 K. A collimated ytterbium beam with flux exceeding $10^{14}$ atoms/s at 823 K is generated using a hexagonally packed capillary nozzle array, with the enhanced thermal response enabling faster experimental cycles for quantum gas and precision metrology work.
motivation: Conventional resistive heating of atomic crucibles in cold atom experiments requires hours to heat or cool, creating substantial apparatus dead time that limits experimental efficiency for high-temperature species like Yb, Er, and Dy operating at 700–1200 K.
method: A water-cooled copper induction coil at 65 mm winding diameter drives eddy currents in a 304 stainless steel crucible with optimized wall thickness matched to the electromagnetic skin depth $\delta = \sqrt{2\rho/\omega\mu}$, directly heating the crucible rather than relying on thermal contact conductance; temperature is stabilized by PI feedback with pulse-width modulation control.
result: At 823 K crucible temperature, the source produces a collimated Yb beam with velocity spread $\pm 72$ m/s and isotopic flux measured via resonance fluorescence of $10^{14}$ atoms/s, following expected Arrhenius vapor-pressure scaling across the 373–1273 K range.
